notes.front: What is the Manifesto for Agile Software Development?
notes.back: A short 2001 declaration, signed by seventeen software practitioners, of four value statements, with twelve principles behind it.
notes.explanation: Its authors present the values as what they came to value through their own work; Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, the authors of the Scrum Guide, are among the signatories.
notes.example: Like a one-page charter a group of practitioners signs, but it names no roles, events or artifacts, which is where the Scrum Guide differs.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In its one-paragraph summary, the Scrum Guide says Scrum requires a {{c1::Scrum Master}} to foster an environment where the Product Owner orders the work, the Scrum Team builds an Increment in a Sprint, and everyone inspects and adjusts.
notes.explanation: The summary ends with “Repeat”: the Scrum Master fosters the conditions for that cycle, not one step of it.
notes.evidence: In a nutshell, Scrum requires a Scrum Master to foster an environment where:

notes.front: A director tells a newly hired Scrum Master: “Your job is to make the team follow the process.” Which description of the Scrum Master’s part matches the Scrum Guide’s summary of Scrum?
notes.back: C: fostering an environment where work is ordered, turned into Increments, inspected and adjusted.
notes.choices:
A) Enforcing the process and reporting team members who do not follow it
B) Ordering the Product Backlog whenever the Product Owner is busy
C) Fostering an environment where the Product Owner orders the work, the team turns it into Increments, and everyone inspects and adjusts
D) Approving each Increment before stakeholders may see it
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide describes fostering an environment, not policing individuals. B: ordering the Product Backlog is the Product Owner’s part of the cycle. D: nothing in the summary makes the Scrum Master an approver of Increments.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s summary gives the ordering, building and inspecting to others; the Scrum Master’s part is the environment in which they happen.
notes.evidence: In a nutshell, Scrum requires a Scrum Master to foster an environment where:

notes.front: In what sense does the Scrum Guide call the Scrum framework “purposefully incomplete”?
notes.back: It defines only the parts required to implement Scrum theory; the collective intelligence of the people using it builds on it.
notes.explanation: A team looking in the Guide for step-by-step working instructions will not find them: that detail is left to the people using Scrum.
notes.evidence: The Scrum framework is purposefully incomplete, only defining the parts required to implement Scrum theory. Scrum is built upon by the collective intelligence of the people using it. Rather than provide people with detailed instructions, the rules of Scrum guide their relationships and interactions.

notes.front: Rather than provide people with detailed instructions, the rules of Scrum guide their {{c1::relationships and interactions}}.
notes.explanation: The rules shape how people work together, leaving the detailed working methods to the people using Scrum.
notes.evidence: The Scrum framework is purposefully incomplete, only defining the parts required to implement Scrum theory. Scrum is built upon by the collective intelligence of the people using it. Rather than provide people with detailed instructions, the rules of Scrum guide their relationships and interactions.

notes.front: What does the Scrum Guide say Scrum does to existing practices?
notes.back: It wraps around them or renders them unnecessary; various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework.
notes.explanation: Scrum is a framework to work inside, so a practice the Guide does not mention may still have a place within it.
notes.evidence: Various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework. Scrum wraps around existing practices or renders them unnecessary.

notes.front: The Developers want to try pair programming and a visual map of their Product Backlog. A colleague objects: “Neither is in the Scrum Guide, so it isn’t Scrum.” What should the Scrum Master say?
notes.back: D: Scrum is purposefully incomplete; various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework
notes.choices:
A) The colleague is right: only practices named in the Scrum Guide are allowed
B) The practices are fine, but the Product Owner must approve each one first
C) The organisation should add the practices to its own edition of the Scrum Guide
D) Scrum is purposefully incomplete; various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide says it defines only the parts required to implement Scrum theory and that other methods can be used within it. B: the Guide gives the Product Owner no such approval right over how the team works. C: the Guide expects practices to be used within the framework, not written into it.
notes.explanation: The Guide leaves room on purpose: Scrum is built upon by the collective intelligence of the people using it.
notes.evidence: Various processes, techniques and methods can be employed within the framework.

notes.front: According to the Scrum Guide, what does Scrum make visible?
notes.back: The relative efficacy of current management, environment and work techniques.
notes.explanation: The Guide gives the purpose in the same sentence: making them visible is what allows improvements to be made.
notes.evidence: Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of current management, environment, and work techniques, so that improvements can be made.

notes.front: After three Sprints, it is clear that every release waits two weeks for sign-off from a separate review board. A manager says: “Scrum is slowing us down.” What is the Scrum Master’s best response?
notes.back: B: explain that Scrum has made the delay visible, and work with the organisation to improve it.
notes.choices:
A) Lengthen the Sprints so that each one includes the two-week sign-off
B) Explain that Scrum makes the efficacy of current management and work techniques visible, and work with the organisation on the sign-off delay
C) Stop holding Sprint Reviews until the board works faster
D) Agree that Scrum does not fit and return to the previous process
notes.choicesExplained: A: this bends Scrum around the problem it has just exposed instead of improving the problem. C: dropping an event removes an opportunity to inspect and adapt and does nothing about the delay. D: the delay existed before Scrum; Scrum only made it visible so that it can be improved.
notes.explanation: Visibility is the point: the Guide says Scrum shows how well current management and techniques work so that improvements can be made.
notes.evidence: Scrum makes visible the relative efficacy of current management, environment, and work techniques, so that improvements can be made.

notes.front: A sponsor wants a detailed twelve-month plan and a single delivery at the end, “so that the project is predictable”. What should the Scrum Master help the sponsor understand?
notes.back: D: Scrum’s iterative, incremental approach is itself meant to optimise predictability and control risk.
notes.choices:
A) Scrum gives up predictability in exchange for speed
B) A twelve-month Sprint would satisfy both the sponsor and Scrum
C) Predictability comes from fixing the full scope before the first Sprint
D) Scrum’s iterative, incremental approach is meant to optimise predictability and control risk, through Increments that can be inspected along the way
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Guide states the opposite aim: the approach is there to optimise predictability. C: Scrum rests on empiricism, where decisions come from what is observed, not from a fixed upfront plan. B: Sprints are one month or less; one long Sprint would remove the iterations that give predictability.
notes.explanation: Each iteration produces something that can be observed, which is what empiricism needs for decisions.
notes.evidence: Scrum employs an iterative, incremental approach to optimize predictability and to control risk.

notes.front: What can artifacts with low transparency lead to, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: Decisions that diminish value and increase risk.
notes.explanation: Important decisions in Scrum rest on the perceived state of the three artifacts, so an unclear artifact misleads the people deciding.
notes.evidence: With Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of its three formal artifacts. Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

notes.front: Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is {{c1::misleading and wasteful}}.
notes.explanation: Inspecting something people cannot see clearly gives a false picture, so the effort spent on it is lost.
notes.evidence: Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.

notes.front: To keep their burn-up chart looking healthy, the Developers mark items as finished in the Sprint Backlog while testing is still pending. The Sprint Review is in two days. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: C: help the Developers make the real state of the work visible before it is inspected.
notes.choices:
A) Let the Sprint Review go ahead and correct the chart afterwards
B) Report the true status privately to management only
C) Raise it with the Developers so that the real state of the work is visible, because inspecting a misleading picture is wasteful
D) Delete the burn-up chart so that nobody is misled
notes.choicesExplained: A: stakeholders would inspect a false picture, which the Guide calls misleading and wasteful. B: the Sprint Backlog must be transparent to those doing and receiving the work, not only to managers. D: removing information reduces transparency further instead of restoring it.
notes.explanation: Transparency comes before inspection: the Sprint Review can only be useful if the work shown is what it seems.
notes.evidence: Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.

notes.front: Senior stakeholders decide next year’s funding from the Product Backlog, but most of its items are vague titles that only the Product Owner understands. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: A: help the Product Owner make the Product Backlog transparent before decisions are made from it.
notes.choices:
A) Help the Product Owner make the Product Backlog transparent, since low-transparency artifacts can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk
B) Rewrite the Product Backlog items personally over a weekend
C) Stop stakeholders from seeing the Product Backlog until it is tidy
D) Do nothing, since the Product Backlog is the Product Owner’s accountability
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Product Owner stays accountable for the Product Backlog; the Scrum Master helps rather than takes over. C: hiding the artifact lowers transparency further. D: the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner and cannot ignore a risk to decisions.
notes.explanation: Funding decisions are important decisions, and the Guide says those rest on the perceived state of the artifacts.
notes.evidence: With Scrum, important decisions are based on the perceived state of its three formal artifacts. Artifacts that have low transparency can lead to decisions that diminish value and increase risk.

notes.front: Inspection enables adaptation. Inspection without adaptation is considered {{c1::pointless}}.
notes.explanation: The Guide adds that Scrum events are designed to provoke change, so an event that changes nothing has missed its point.
notes.evidence: Inspection enables adaptation. Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless. Scrum events are designed to provoke change.

notes.front: What are Scrum events designed to do, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: Provoke change.
notes.explanation: Scrum gives inspection a cadence through its five events, and inspection is meant to enable adaptation.
notes.evidence: To help with inspection, Scrum provides cadence in the form of its five events. Inspection enables adaptation. Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless. Scrum events are designed to provoke change.

notes.front: Stakeholders give detailed feedback at every Sprint Review, yet the Product Backlog has not changed in months. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: D: help the Scrum Team act on what the Sprint Review inspects, since inspection without adaptation is pointless.
notes.choices:
A) Add the feedback to the Product Backlog personally
B) Nothing, as long as the Sprint Review happens every Sprint
C) Ask stakeholders to send feedback by email instead
D) Help the Scrum Team see that inspection without adaptation is pointless, and that the Sprint Review should lead to changes where the feedback warrants them
notes.choicesExplained: B: holding the event is not enough; events are designed to provoke change. C: changing the channel does not make the team adapt to what it learns. A: the Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog; the Scrum Master helps the team adapt rather than doing it for them.
notes.explanation: A Sprint Review that never changes anything is an inspection with no adaptation, which the Guide calls pointless.
notes.evidence: Inspection enables adaptation. Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless. Scrum events are designed to provoke change.

notes.front: A Scrum Team is expected to adapt {{c1::the moment it learns anything new}} through inspection.
notes.explanation: What a team learns is not saved for the next scheduled event: adjustments are to be made as soon as possible to minimise further deviation.
notes.evidence: The adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation. Adaptation becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing. A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection.

notes.front: On day three of a two-week Sprint, the Developers find that their chosen technical approach cannot meet the Definition of Done. One says: “Let’s raise it at the Sprint Retrospective.” What should the Scrum Master encourage?
notes.back: C: adapt the plan now, bringing in the Product Owner if scope must be renegotiated.
notes.choices:
A) Waiting for the Sprint Retrospective, since that is the event for process changes
B) Extending the Sprint by a week to absorb the problem
C) Adapting the plan now, involving the Product Owner if the scope needs renegotiating
D) The Scrum Master choosing a new technical approach for them
notes.choicesExplained: A: the adjustment must be made as soon as possible; waiting lets the deviation grow. B: Sprints are fixed-length events of one month or less. D: how to turn the work into an Increment is for the Developers to decide.
notes.explanation: The team has learnt something new through inspection, and the Guide expects adaptation at that moment rather than at a later event.
notes.evidence: The adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation. Adaptation becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing. A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection.

notes.front: Every change to the Sprint Backlog must be approved by a department manager, who reviews requests once a week. The Developers learn something that changes their plan almost daily. What should the Scrum Master do?
notes.back: B: work with the manager so the Developers can adapt their own plan.
notes.choices:
A) Collect the changes and submit them together at the weekly review
B) Work with the manager so that the Developers can adapt their own plan, since adaptation is harder when people are not empowered or self-managing
C) Approve the changes on the manager’s behalf
D) Ask the Developers to stop updating the Sprint Backlog mid-Sprint
notes.choicesExplained: A: batching delays adjustments the Guide says must be made as soon as possible. C: this swaps one approver for another; the Developers are still not self-managing their plan. D: the Sprint Backlog is updated throughout the Sprint as more is learned.
notes.explanation: Approval queues put the people who learn something away from the decision, which the Guide says makes adaptation more difficult.
notes.evidence: The adjustment must be made as soon as possible to minimize further deviation. Adaptation becomes more difficult when the people involved are not empowered or self-managing. A Scrum Team is expected to adapt the moment it learns anything new through inspection.

notes.front: Under the Scrum value of Respect, how do Scrum Team members regard each other?
notes.back: As capable, independent people; and they are respected as such by the people they work with.
notes.explanation: Respect runs both ways: among team members, and from the people the team works with.
notes.evidence: Scrum Team members respect each other to be capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people with whom they work.

notes.front: A Developer has been stuck for a week but tells stakeholders that everything is on track, fearing she will look incompetent. Which Scrum value is most directly missing?
notes.back: D: Openness
notes.choices:
A) Focus
B) Respect
C) Commitment
D) Openness
notes.choicesExplained: A: she is working on the Sprint’s work; the gap is in what she shares about it. B: nobody is treated as less than capable here; the issue is concealment. C: she is still trying to reach the goal; she is hiding the challenge, not abandoning it.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks the Scrum Team and its stakeholders to be open about the work and the challenges, and a hidden blocker is a hidden challenge.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team and its stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges.

notes.front: Midway through the Sprint, a Developer spends most of his time on favours for another department, unrelated to the Sprint Goal. Which Scrum value is most directly at stake?
notes.back: B: Focus
notes.choices:
A) Courage
B) Focus
C) Openness
D) Respect
notes.choicesExplained: A: no tough problem is being avoided; the attention is simply elsewhere. C: the work is visible; the issue is where his attention goes. D: the favours do not treat anyone as less capable.
notes.explanation: The Guide makes the work of the Sprint the primary focus, to make the best possible progress toward the team’s goals.
notes.evidence: Their primary focus is on the work of the Sprint to make the best possible progress toward these goals.

notes.front: Everyone on the Scrum Team knows a director’s deadline can only be met by skipping agreed quality checks, but nobody is willing to raise it with the director. Which Scrum value is most directly lacking?
notes.back: A: Courage
notes.choices:
A) Courage
B) Respect
C) Focus
D) Commitment
notes.choicesExplained: C: the team is focused on the work; what is missing is the will to raise a hard issue. B: the director is not being disrespected; the problem is avoided. D: the team still wants to reach the goal; the gap is in facing the problem.
notes.explanation: The Guide describes courage as doing the right thing and working on tough problems, and this is both.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team members have the courage to do the right thing, to work on tough problems.

notes.front: A senior Developer rewrites colleagues’ work overnight and openly tells the team they “can’t be trusted with the hard parts”. Which Scrum value is most directly undermined?
notes.back: B: Respect
notes.choices:
A) Focus
B) Respect
C) Courage
D) Openness
notes.choicesExplained: A: he is working hard on the Sprint’s work; the harm is to how he regards others. C: he is not avoiding tough problems; he is taking them from others. D: his view is stated openly; the issue is that it treats colleagues as incapable.
notes.explanation: Under Respect, team members regard each other as capable, independent people.
notes.evidence: Scrum Team members respect each other to be capable, independent people, and are respected as such by the people with whom they work.

notes.front: One Developer is blocked on the item most critical to the Sprint Goal. The others, having finished their own items, start personal learning projects instead of helping. Which Scrum value is most directly missing?
notes.back: B: Commitment
notes.choices:
A) Openness
B) Commitment
C) Respect
D) Courage
notes.choicesExplained: A: the blocker is known to everyone; the gap is in supporting the colleague. C: nobody is treating the colleague as incapable; they are just not helping. D: no one is avoiding a difficult conversation; they are not pulling together toward the goal.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s Commitment covers both achieving the team’s goals and supporting each other, and neither is happening here.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team commits to achieving its goals and to supporting each other.

notes.front: What do the Scrum values give direction to, according to the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: The Scrum Team’s work, actions and behaviour.
notes.explanation: The values are meant to show in how the team works and behaves day to day, not only in what it says.
notes.evidence: These values give direction to the Scrum Team with regard to their work, actions, and behavior.

notes.front: A manager plans to publish a weekly ranking of each Developer’s completed items “to boost commitment”. What should the Scrum Master raise first?
notes.back: D: the way Scrum is used should reinforce the values, and the ranking may undermine them.
notes.choices:
A) The Scrum Master should produce the ranking to keep it fair
B) A ranking is fine as long as it is shared only with the Product Owner
C) Rankings should use hours worked instead of completed items
D) The way Scrum is used should reinforce the values; a ranking that sets team-mates against each other may undermine commitment to supporting each other
notes.choicesExplained: B: hiding the ranking does not change its effect on how team members treat each other. C: the problem is ranking individuals against each other, not the measure chosen. A: this makes the Scrum Master the source of the practice that may undermine the values.
notes.explanation: Commitment in the Guide includes supporting each other, and a practice that rewards individuals against each other pulls the other way.
notes.evidence: The decisions that are made, the steps taken, and the way Scrum is used should reinforce these values, not diminish or undermine them.

notes.front: How do Scrum Team members learn and explore the Scrum values, according to the Guide?
notes.back: As they work with the Scrum events and artifacts.
notes.explanation: The values are learnt in practice, through the work of Scrum itself, rather than in a separate course.
notes.evidence: The Scrum Team members learn and explore the values as they work with the Scrum events and artifacts.

notes.front: What happens when the Scrum values are embodied by the Scrum Team and the people they work with?
notes.back: The pillars of transparency, inspection and adaptation come to life, building trust.
notes.explanation: The Guide includes the people the team works with, so building trust is not the team’s job alone.
notes.evidence: When these values are embodied by the Scrum Team and the people they work with, the empirical Scrum pillars of transparency, inspection, and adaptation come to life building trust.

notes.front: Stakeholders distrust the Scrum Team and demand daily written status reports. The team, in turn, hides problems to look good. What approach best fits the Scrum Guide?
notes.back: B: help the team and stakeholders live the values so that the pillars come to life and trust builds.
notes.choices:
A) Provide the daily reports, written by the Scrum Master
B) Help both the team and its stakeholders live the values, such as openness about the work and the challenges, so the pillars come to life and trust builds
C) Coach the team to share only good news until confidence grows
D) Keep stakeholders away from the team until trust returns
notes.choicesExplained: A: more reporting does not address the hidden problems, and it bypasses openness between the team and stakeholders. D: trust is built when values are embodied by the team and the people they work with, which needs contact. C: this deepens the lack of openness that caused the distrust.
notes.explanation: The Guide ties trust to values embodied by the team and the people it works with, so both sides are part of the answer.
notes.evidence: When these values are embodied by the Scrum Team and the people they work with, the empirical Scrum pillars of transparency, inspection, and adaptation come to life building trust.

notes.front: Which failure does the Scrum Guide call “misleading and wasteful”, and which does it call “pointless”?
notes.back: Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful; inspection without adaptation is pointless.
notes.explanation: The pillars depend on each other in sequence: transparency enables inspection, and inspection enables adaptation.
notes.evidence: Transparency enables inspection. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful. Inspection The Scrum artifacts and the progress toward agreed goals must be inspected frequently and diligently to detect potentially undesirable variances or problems. To help with inspection, Scrum provides cadence in the form of its five events. Inspection enables adaptation. Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless.

notes.front: How did the authors of the Manifesto for Agile Software Development say they arrived at its values?
notes.back: By developing software themselves and helping others to do it.
notes.explanation: The values are presented as lessons drawn from practice, still being uncovered, rather than as a finished theory.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Manifesto for Agile Software Development, what is valued more than processes and tools?
notes.back: Individuals and interactions.
notes.explanation: People and the way they work together come first; processes and tools stay on the list as things of value.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Manifesto for Agile Software Development, what is valued more than comprehensive documentation?
notes.back: Working software.
notes.explanation: The comparison is with documentation that is comprehensive; the Manifesto ranks a product that works above it.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Manifesto for Agile Software Development, what is valued more than contract negotiation?
notes.back: Customer collaboration.
notes.explanation: Working with the customer is ranked above bargaining over terms with them, though contracts keep their place.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the Manifesto for Agile Software Development, what is valued more than following a plan?
notes.back: Responding to change.
notes.explanation: Plans still have value; when the situation changes, adjusting is ranked above sticking to the original plan.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does the Manifesto for Agile Software Development reject processes, documentation, contracts and plans?
notes.back: No. It says the items on the right have value; the items on the left are simply valued more.
notes.explanation: The Manifesto sets out preferences between two good things, not a ban on the second.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A Developer argues: “We are agile now, so we stop writing any documentation.” How should the Scrum Master respond, drawing on the Manifesto for Agile Software Development?
notes.back: C: working software is valued more than comprehensive documentation, but documentation still has value.
notes.choices:
A) Agree: the Manifesto rejects documentation
B) Insist on documenting everything, since the Manifesto values documentation most
C) The Manifesto values working software more than comprehensive documentation, but it still says documentation has value
D) Say the Manifesto does not mention documentation at all
notes.choicesExplained: A: the Manifesto says there is value in the items on the right, including documentation. B: the Manifesto ranks working software above comprehensive documentation. D: documentation appears in one of its four value statements.
notes.explanation: The Manifesto ranks pairs of good things; neither side of a pair is thrown away.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do the principles behind the Agile Manifesto name as the highest priority?
notes.back: Satisfying the customer by delivering valuable software early and continuously.
notes.explanation: Customer satisfaction is tied to delivery, early and ongoing, rather than to a single hand-over at the end.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What stance do the Agile principles take on requirements that change late in development?
notes.back: Welcome them; agile processes use change to give the customer a competitive advantage.
notes.explanation: Late change is treated as an opportunity for the customer rather than a disruption to be resisted.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How often do the Agile principles ask for working software to be delivered?
notes.back: Frequently: every couple of weeks to every couple of months, preferring the shorter end.
notes.explanation: The range is wide, but the principle leans toward the shorter timescale.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the Agile principles, how often must business people and developers work together?
notes.back: Daily, throughout the project.
notes.explanation: The principle asks for daily joint work across the whole project, not only at the start and the end.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the Agile principles, what should projects be built around, and what should those people be given?
notes.back: Motivated individuals; the environment and support they need, and trust to get the job done.
notes.explanation: The principle pairs support with trust: people get what they need and are then trusted to deliver.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which way of conveying information to and within a development team do the Agile principles call the most efficient and effective?
notes.back: Face-to-face conversation.
notes.explanation: The principle ranks talking directly above other ways of passing information within and to a team.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do the Agile principles call the primary measure of progress?
notes.back: Working software.
notes.explanation: Progress is judged by what works, not by activity such as documents written or hours spent.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What kind of pace do the Agile principles say sponsors, developers and users should be able to keep up?
notes.back: A constant pace, indefinitely: agile processes promote sustainable development.
notes.explanation: The principle names sponsors and users alongside developers, so a sustainable pace concerns everyone involved.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the Agile principles, what enhances agility?
notes.back: Continuous attention to technical excellence and good design.
notes.explanation: The principle links agility to quality of design, not only to speed of delivery.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How do the Agile principles define simplicity?
notes.back: The art of maximising the amount of work not done; they call it essential.
notes.explanation: Simplicity is framed as skill in leaving out work, not as doing the same work more simply.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: According to the Agile principles, where do the best architectures, requirements and designs come from?
notes.back: They emerge from teams that organise themselves.
notes.explanation: The principle says the best designs emerge from the team rather than being handed to it.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What do the Agile principles ask a team to do at regular intervals?
notes.back: Reflect on how to become more effective, then tune and adjust its behaviour.
notes.explanation: Reflection is only half of it: the principle expects the team to change its behaviour as a result.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team has worked late nights and weekends in every Sprint for six months, and two people have gone on sick leave. Which Agile principle does this most directly go against?
notes.back: D: the principle of sustainable development at a constant pace.
notes.choices:
A) Welcoming changing requirements, even late in development
B) Simplicity: maximising the amount of work not done
C) Working software is the primary measure of progress
D) Agile processes promote sustainable development, at a pace everyone can keep up indefinitely
notes.choicesExplained: B: the problem is the pace of work, not how much unnecessary work is done. C: the team may well be producing working software; the pace is what cannot last. A: nothing here concerns changing requirements.
notes.explanation: The principle asks for a pace that can be kept up indefinitely, and this one is already breaking people.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A programme reports progress as the percentage of design documents signed off, with no working software yet after eight months. Which Agile principle does this reporting most directly go against?
notes.back: B: Working software is the primary measure of progress
notes.choices:
A) Business people and developers must work together daily
B) Working software is the primary measure of progress
C) Face-to-face conversation is the most effective way to convey information
D) Continuous attention to technical excellence enhances agility
notes.choicesExplained: A: the issue is how progress is measured, not who works together. C: the medium of communication is not the problem here. D: good design matters, but the reporting problem is measuring documents instead of working software.
notes.explanation: Signed-off documents are activity; the principle measures progress by what actually works.
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
